message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This review is grounded in two months of actual till data for every main course, a full competitor price check, and the latest supplier information, so the recommendations are not guesswork. The price increases are modest and targeted: each of the three dishes stays below the midpoint of competitor prices for that dish, so we remain the value option in the area, and with 60% of bookings from repeat guests our customer base is loyal enough to absorb a pound or two. The projected effect is simple to check, £810 a week or about £42,000 a year in additional gross profit, which lifts our main-course margin to about 71%. I also think the menu-mix decision is clear-cut: the data show the mushroom risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so replacing it with a seasonal special is an easy improvement. Monitoring for eight weeks gives us an early warning if volumes move. Overall I believe these changes are sensible, low-risk and well evidenced.
</author>

<document>
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.
</document>
response:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Verdict:** The price increases look reasonable and sit within competitor ranges. However, the case for removing the mushroom risotto rests on a misreading of Table 1, since the risotto has the *highest* margin on the menu. The £42,000 gain also ignores the 12% beef price rise reported in the paper itself. Once both are corrected, the real gain is roughly a third to a half of the figure presented.

## 1. The risotto has the best margin, not the weakest

Table 1 shows:

| Dish | Margin % | Cash profit per plate |
|---|---|---|
| **Mushroom risotto** | **80%** (highest) | £11.20 |
| Chicken curry | 75% | £10.90 |
| Beef burger | 72% | £10.80 |
| Fish and chips | 69% | £11.40 |
| Sirloin steak | 60% | £15.60 |
| Specials | 64% | various |

Even in cash terms, the risotto earns more per plate than the curry or the burger. Its sales of 90 plates a week are tied for lowest with the specials, so "lowest sales" is only partly true. The claim that it "has the weakest margin" appears in section 5.2 and in the author's summary, and it's the opposite of what the data show.

**Replacing it could cost money.** If the seasonal vegetarian special performs like current specials at 64%, swapping it for the risotto at the same price and volume reduces gross profit by about **£200 a week**:

90 plates × £14 × (80% − 64%) ≈ £202, or **about £10,500 a year**

It's also worth checking whether the risotto is the only standing vegetarian main. If it is, removing it could affect group bookings that include vegetarians.

## 2. The £42,000 gain ignores the beef price rise

The arithmetic checks out *if costs stay the same*:
- £1 × 310 + £1 × 260 + £2 × 120 = **£810 a week**
- £810 × 52 = **£42,120 a year**

But section 4 reports that **beef prices rise 12% from 1 April**, the same day as the new prices. If the full plate cost of the burger and steak moved with beef, which is an upper bound since sides and buns won't rise:

| Dish | Extra food cost per plate | Plates | Weekly cost increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burger | £4.20 × 12% ≈ £0.50 | 260 | ≈ £131 |
| Steak | £10.40 × 12% ≈ £1.25 | 120 | ≈ £150 |
| **Total** | | | **≈ £281** |

**Net weekly gain:** £810 − £281 ≈ **£529**, or about **£27,500 a year**. The real figure is somewhere between this and £42,000, depending on how much of each plate is beef. The paper should show the calculation.

If the risotto is also replaced at a 64% margin, the gain falls to about **£330 a week, or roughly £17,000 a year**.

## 3. The 71% margin figure doesn't hold up

Using Table 1 and leaving out the specials, whose revenue isn't given:

| Scenario | Main-course margin |
|---|---|
| Today | about 69.9% |
| New prices, costs unchanged | about 71.3%, the paper's figure |
| New prices, with the beef rise | about 69.7% |
| Also replacing the risotto with a 64% special | about 68.5% |

So the claimed lift to 71% depends on beef costs staying the same, which section 4 says won't happen. In practice the main-course margin stays at about **70%** or slips slightly.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Trading days:** the restaurant opens Wednesday to Sunday, which is **five** days, but section 8 refers to "six trading days a week." This doesn't change the weekly figures but should be corrected.
- **"Remain the value option":** before the change, all three dishes are the cheapest in the group. Afterwards, each is above the cheapest competitor (£17.50 against £16.95, £16 against £15.50, £28 against £27). They're still below the midpoint, but no longer cheapest.
- **Monitoring baseline:** comparing April and May against January and February will pick up seasonal changes, since spring trade is usually stronger. A year-on-year comparison, or tracking covers alongside plates per dish, would give a clearer signal.
- **Volume assumptions:** "volumes hold" rests on the 2024 price change having "no visible effect on bookings," which is thin evidence. Repeat guests are also the ones most likely to *notice* an increase. A scenario with, say, 5% lower volume on the three dishes would make the case more robust.
- **Weekday lunch:** the paper says it's "a small share" but gives no figure.

## What holds up

- Table 1's margins and volumes are correct and add to 1,050.
- All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints:
  - fish and chips £17.50, against a midpoint of £17.98
  - burger £16.00, against £16.50
  - steak £28.00, against £29.50
- Raising prices that haven't changed since September 2024 is reasonable, especially for beef dishes facing a cost increase.
- Weekly monitoring is a good idea.

## Recommended changes

1. **Keep the risotto,** or justify its removal on grounds other than margin. Note that it has the highest margin on the menu.
2. **Include the beef cost rise** in the projection and show the net gain, likely between about £27,500 and £42,000 a year.
3. **Recalculate the margin effect,** which is about 70% rather than 71% once the beef rise is included.
4. **Correct "six trading days"** to five.
5. **Add a volume-sensitivity scenario,** and compare monitoring results year-on-year rather than against January and February.

The price increases themselves are defensible. Making them alongside a cost rise is exactly why they're needed. The paper just needs to show the net effect honestly and drop the risotto proposal unless there's another reason for it.
